newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq cuts food rations, blames Washington.
newsitem.headline: Iraq cuts food rations, blames Washington.

text.p: Iraq cut food rations for its people on Thursday, saying it would not be able to meet all food quotas agreed upon under its oil deal with the United Nations, and blaming the United States for the shortfall.

Apart from wheat flour, the amount of other essentials like rice, sugar, tea and detergents handed out to Iraqis at giveaway prices will be on average 50 per cent below quantities based on the sharply down on quantities foreseen under the oil deal.
The Iraqi News Agency (INA) said each Iraqi will get half a kg (one lb) of sugar in June instead of two and 1.25 kg of rice instead of 2.5.

"The reason not to increase rations of rice, sugar, tea and detergents in June...is due to the attitude of American administration which cancelled a rice contract with Vietnam and held up four other ones," INA said, quoting an official source at the trade ministry.
Millions of Iraqis rely on government food rations for survival and many thought the increased rations under the oil deal would help them make ends meet.
Iraq started exporting oil on December 10 but while the oil exports have gone on smoothly, food and medicine have not been reaching the country on time.

Under the deal Iraq is allowed exports of $2 billion in six months. The current pact comes under review on June 9 and the trade ministry source said Iraq now had more than $160 million in its escrow account at the United Nations.
Only a truckload of 61 tonnes of medicine has reached the country so far and about 720,000 tonnes of food out of more than two million tonnes Iraq has contracted for.
The source said only one shipment of sugar had arrived so far in Iraq "which does not secure the distribution of two kilogrammes for each person" as the deal calls for.
It said the U.S. had cancelled two sugar contracts and held up two more. Iraq is under U.N. sanctions for invading Kuwait in 1990.
The reduced rations are bound to lead to a hike in prices of essential foods on the open market and are likely to boomerang on the value of the local currency.
The source said the trade ministry failed to increase the tea ration because "the American administration cancelled two other contracts and delayed ratification of two more."
"These realities clearly confirm the hostile attitude of the American administration vis-a-vis the Iraqi people and the increased suffering it is causing to them," the source said.
Iraqi officials have frequently accused Washington of blocking food and medical contracts and being behind the delays in the arrival of humanitarian goods.
